claim_verdicts.evidence: task-asynchronous-programming-model.md l.112: "an async method returns a task value when its work is suspended ... When the async method eventually completes its work, the task is marked as completed and the result, if any, is stored in the task." asynchronous-programming/index.md l.193: "When a task that runs asynchronously throws an exception, that task is faulted. The Task object holds the exception thrown in the Task.Exception property." async-return-types.md l.45: Task<TResult> is the type for an async method whose return operand is TResult.

common-async-bugs.md l.23: "Adding the `async` keyword to a method doesn't make the method run on a background thread. It tells the compiler to allow `await` inside the method body and to wrap the return value in a Task." task-asynchronous-programming-model.md l.124: "The `async` and `await` keywords don't cause extra threads to be created. Async methods don't require multithreading because an async method doesn't run on its own thread."

common-async-bugs.md l.23, word for word: "When you invoke an async method, it runs synchronously until it reaches the first `await` on an incomplete awaitable. If the method contains no `await` expressions, or if every awaitable it awaits is already complete, the method completes entirely on the calling thread."

task-asynchronous-programming-model.md l.122: "An `await` expression in an async method doesn't block the current thread while the awaited task is running. Instead, the expression signs up the rest of the method as a continuation and returns control to the caller of the async method." Same page l.132: the `await` operator "tells the compiler that the async method can't continue past that point until the awaited asynchronous process is complete. In the meantime, control returns to the caller."

synchronizationcontext-console-apps.md l.19: "Console apps don't install a SynchronizationContext, which means `await` continuations run on the thread pool." l.23: "In a console app, SynchronizationContext.Current returns null. When a method yields at an `await`, the continuation runs on whatever thread pool thread is available"; the page's sample output shows thread 1 before the first yield and threads 2399-2687 afterwards.

operators/await.md l.32: "The type of expression `await t` is `TResult` if the type of expression `t` is Task<TResult> or ValueTask<TResult>. ... In both cases, if `t` throws an exception, `await t` rethrows the exception." On ordinary control flow, task-asynchronous-programming-model.md l.76: "Some routine processes, such as loops and exception handling, can be difficult to handle in traditional asynchronous code. In an async method, you write these elements much as you would in a synchronous solution."

common-async-bugs.md, section "Missing await on a task-returning call": "If you call a task-returning method in an `async` method without awaiting it, the method starts the asynchronous operation but doesn't wait for it to complete." The other half (what the caller is handed) is l.23: the call runs synchronously up to the first incomplete await, at which point the unfinished task is returned.
claim_verdicts.source: refs/dotnet-docs/docs/standard/asynchronous-programming-patterns/common-async-bugs.md l.23, section 'Missing await on a task-returning call'

First half exact: operators/await.md l.28: "You can use the `await` operator only in a method, lambda expression, or anonymous method that is modified by the `async` keyword." Second half is stated as exhaustive and is not: async-return-types.md l.9-15 lists Task, Task<TResult>, "`void`, for an event handler", any type with an accessible GetAwaiter, and IAsyncEnumerable<T>; and 'Void return type' says "an async method that returns void can't be awaited". So "plain Task when it gives nothing, so the caller can await it either way" holds only outside async void.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: A method that uses await must itself be marked async, and an async method does not hand back a plain value: its declared return type is a task type — Task<TResult> here — when it gives a value back, and plain Task when it gives nothing, so the caller can await it either way. Awaiting spreads outwards to every caller.

claim_verdicts.evidence: async-return-types.md, 'Task<TResult> return type': "The Task<TResult> return type is used for an async method that contains a return statement in which the operand is TResult. ... the await expression retrieves the integer value ... stored in the task returned by the method." task-asynchronous-programming-model.md l.112: "the task is marked as completed and the result, if any, is stored in the task." Declared type is the task; the return operand is the TResult.

issues.text: "a request hangs forever" is false on the pinned stack. The deadlock needs a single-threaded SynchronizationContext (common-async-bugs.md), and CA2007 states: "when writing code in an ASP.NET Core application, by default there is no SynchronizationContext or TaskScheduler." The doc deadlock sequence says "the UI thread (or an ASP.NET request thread in older ASP.NET)" — legacy ASP.NET, never taught here. versions.yaml pins aspnetcore 10.0 and related points at backend.l1.request-lifecycle, so the reader maps "a request" onto ASP.NET Core and learns a symptom that stack cannot produce.
issues.fix: Drop the request half: "You notice this when a screen hangs forever with no error at all, or when the error names `AggregateException` and the message you need sits in its `InnerException`." If a server symptom is wanted, say instead that on a server `.Result` costs a held thread rather than a hang. Nothing else in the lesson depends on the word "request".
issues.quote: You notice this when a screen or a request hangs forever with no error at all

Claim 13 carries the same over-reach and is marked `rephrased`.
issues.fix: Bound the sentence to methods that return a task, e.g.: "…and an `async` method that returns something hands back a task carrying the value, or plain `Task` when there is nothing, so its caller can `await` it and know when it ended." issues.text: Two inaccuracies in one clause. It is the compiler, not the runtime, that arranges disposal — statements/using.md: "The compiler rewrites it into a try/finally, so the resource's Dispose is always called"; and disposal happens "at the end of the scope in which it's declared", not at the end of the method (the two coincide here only because the declarations sit in the method body). Claim 21 is worded correctly with "enclosing scope"; the lesson text drifts from its own claim.
